name: CARE USA: humanitarian and development programmes (charityevals' estimate)
beneficiaries_note: Our build: CARE USA's spending abroad by region from its Form 990 Schedule F Part I (Sub-Saharan Africa 61%, the Middle East and North Africa 17%, South Asia 10%, East Asia and the Pacific 4%, Europe 4% (Turkey and Ukraine), Central America and the Caribbean 3%, South America 1%), each region split equally over CARE's main programme countries there (a judgment: no country split is published); public information aims at the same people.
summary: CARE USA spent $748 million on programmes in its fiscal year to June 2025: $397 million on emergency response (largest in Ethiopia, Turkey, Yemen and Sudan), $344 million on development (food security, health, savings groups for women, water and education) and $7 million on public information, mostly through its own country offices and local partners. CARE reports people reached for the whole confederation but no outcome data for its own spending, so every branch is built from spending, a judged cost per person anchored on the confederation's reach, and the research on that kind of work, and every branch is discounted for missing data. Relief (food, cash and goods for about 15 million people, with a few excess crisis deaths averted) is about three-fifths of the result, savings groups for women about a sixth; the biggest uncertainties are the missing-data discount, how much savings groups raise consumption, and how poor the crisis-affected people are and what others would have given them anyway.

sections.title: Other outcomes, in this model's unit
sections.explainer: charityevals' standard step for outcomes in more than one unit (docs/normalization.md 2.6): each outcome is counted in its own unit (units of value for income and deaths, WELLBYs for life satisfaction, tonnes of CO₂e, chicken pain days) and put into this model's unit by its unit's conversion over this unit's, which the headline's conversion cancels. So each moves only with its own sliders, exactly as in a model of its own unit. The rows are fixed; don't edit them.

rows.label: Share of development spending on health
rows.explainer: CARE USA doesn't split development spending by sector. Anchor: its development grants abroad by purpose (Form 990 Schedule F Part II, purpose codes summed over 670 grants): food, water and nutrition $20.7M, economic growth $15.8M, women and families $10.4M, global health $9.5M, resilient futures $3.3M, other $21.9M. Health is global health (16% of the coded grants) plus about half of women and families (sexual and reproductive health, maternal care): 24% (15-35%).

rows.label: Share of development spending on water, sanitation and hygiene
rows.explainer: Within food, water and nutrition (35% of the coded development grants, Schedule F Part II), water and hygiene is the smaller part: CARE reports 19.8 million people reached by food and water work in fiscal 2024, most of them through food security. 10% (5-18%).

rows.label: Share of development spending on education
rows.explainer: The other half of women and families (17% of the coded grants) is education, girls' leadership and gender-based violence work; CARE reports 13.6 million people reached by education and skills work in fiscal 2024, much of it savings-group skills training. 8% (3-15%).

rows.label: Share of development spending on women's economic empowerment and savings groups
rows.explainer: Economic growth is 26% of the coded development grants (Schedule F Part II): Village Savings and Loan Associations, women's enterprise and market access. 26% (18-34%).

rows.label: Share of development spending on food security, agriculture, nutrition and climate resilience
rows.explainer: The rest: food and nutrition security and farming (the larger part of food, water and nutrition) and climate resilience: about 31%.

rows.label: Health spending per birth covered by maternal and newborn care
rows.explainer: CARE's health work is mostly maternal, newborn and reproductive health through community health workers and clinics: 11.5 million people reached by health work in fiscal 2024 against roughly a quarter of the confederation's $498M of development spending, about $11 a person reached, and about one person reached in twenty is a woman giving birth that year (most are women of reproductive age, a few are children). So about $220 per birth covered; wider work (family planning, adolescents, health systems) raises it. $250 ($100-600).

rows.explainer: CARE's water work is mostly hygiene promotion, community water committees and rehabilitating water points, with fewer new schemes than World Vision's boreholes ($150 there): its food-and-water reach of 19.8 million on about $200M of the confederation's development money is about $10 a person, mostly food work. $60 ($30-150) per person given safer water.

rows.label: Food security, nutrition and resilience spending per person reached
rows.explainer: Farmer training, seeds and inputs, nutrition counselling and resilience work: CARE's food-and-water reach (19.8 million in fiscal 2024, part of it crisis food already in relief) on about $200M of the confederation's development money is $10-20 a person; deeper support for fewer people costs more. $40 ($15-100).

rows.explainer: Farm output and income are shared by the household, as for savings-group members (household_size); but CARE counts participants, and some households have two participants counted (couples in farmer groups) or the gain is the participant's own (nutrition counselling). Half the other members (20-90%).

rows.label: People sharing the food security gains
rows.explainer: Each participant and a share of the rest of the household: about 2.7 people per participant.

rows.label: Education spending per child or young person reached
rows.explainer: Community-based schools (Afghanistan), girls' leadership clubs and adult literacy: CARE's 13.6 million reached by education and skills in fiscal 2024 include short trainings; a child given a year of schooling costs $50-250. $80 ($30-250).

rows.explainer: Children and young people reached by education.

rows.label: Death rate among the people reached during the crisis, without the response
rows.explainer: CARE's largest responses were Ethiopia, Turkey, Yemen and Sudan (note 1), with Gaza, Syria, Afghanistan, Somalia and South Sudan: mortality surveys in the famine-risk settings find crude death rates of 0.3-1 per 10,000 a day (0.011-0.037 a year), while earthquake recovery in Turkey and Syria runs near normal rates. Below World Vision's 0.018, whose relief is mostly food in famine-risk Africa. 0.014 (0.009-0.03).

rows.label: Death rate in the same population before the crisis
rows.explainer: The site's crude death rates for three of CARE's four largest responses (UN World Population Prospects), so only excess deaths count.

rows.label: Share of the excess deaths the response averts among the people reached
rows.explainer: CARE's response is food and cash (US government food aid, WFP), water and hygiene, shelter and protection. The evidence is weak: the Cochrane review of cash in disasters (Pega et al. 2015) found one drought study with far fewer child deaths, very low certainty; long-running cash programmes cut under-five deaths by about 8% (Richterman et al. 2023). Most people reached are not at risk of dying in the months covered. 8% (2-20%), a little under World Vision's 10% because more of CARE's response is in middle-income settings (Turkey, Syria, Ukraine).

rows.label: Years each person is covered by the response
rows.explainer: Distributions and services run a few months for most people reached. 0.25 years (0.1-0.5).

rows.label: Excess deaths averted per person reached
rows.explainer: Excess deaths averted per person reached.

rows.label: Share of the excess deaths averted that are of children under five
rows.explainer: Excess deaths in food crises and displacement are mostly young children's: mortality surveys in crises commonly find under-five death rates about twice the crude rate, and the family guidance gives 40-60% under five. No all-cause age split for CARE's response countries is in the site's facts yet; the diarrhoeal split in Sub-Saharan Africa (55% under five, @death_ages) is inside the range. 50% (40-60%).

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at five or older, share aged 5 to 14
rows.explainer: A stand-in: among deaths over five, the share aged 5-14 in the site's split of diarrhoeal deaths in Sub-Saharan Africa (GBD, facts/death_ages.json), used until an all-cause split for the response countries is in the facts.

rows.label: Of the deaths averted at 15 or older, share aged 15 to 49
rows.explainer: A stand-in: among deaths over fifteen, the share aged 15-49 in the same diarrhoeal split, used until an all-cause split for the response countries is in the facts.

rows.explainer: Food-insecure households in Ethiopia, Sudan, Yemen or Somalia consume well under the stand-ins' survey mean (the poorest fifth about 40% of it); people displaced by Turkey's earthquake or in Ukraine consume more. 60% (35-90%).

rows.explainer: The goods on the site's one log-income scale over the time they are used: they raise consumption during the months each person is covered (years_exposed), so the gain is years_exposed × ln(1 + value ÷ the consumption of that period).

rows.explainer: Maternal complications and deaths averted, family planning's spacing of births, newborn illness: GiveWell's supplementary illness shares for child-health programmes run 5-20% of the mortality value, and CARE's work weighs more towards mothers and reproductive health. 15% (0-40%).

rows.label: Diarrhoeal deaths per person-year, Sub-Saharan Africa (all ages)

source.title: IHME, Global Burden of Disease 2021 results tool (diarrhoeal diseases, Sub-Saharan Africa, all ages, deaths per 100,000)

rows.explainer: The rate a new water supply acts on; wide because the GBD estimate varies by country and year.

rows.label: Fall in diarrhoeal deaths from improved water with hygiene promotion
rows.explainer: Meta-analyses (Wolf et al. 2022, Lancet) find large falls in diarrhoea for piped water and chlorination, small and uncertain ones for improved community sources, and about 30% less diarrhoea for handwashing promotion in trials with lower uptake at scale; CARE's mix is hygiene promotion and community water points. 10% (0-25%) of diarrhoeal deaths.

rows.label: Other deaths averted per diarrhoeal death averted
rows.explainer: The site's shared ratio for water programmes.

rows.label: Years the improved water and hygiene practices last
rows.explainer: Rehabilitated water points last 5-10 years with repairs; handwashing habits fade within a few years without reinforcement. 6 years (3-12), below a new borehole's 10.

rows.label: Share of those years the water point or practice keeps working
rows.explainer: About a quarter to a third of rural water points in Sub-Saharan Africa are broken at any time (Rural Water Supply Network); CARE trains water committees to repair them. 65% (45-85%).

rows.label: Working years of the water and hygiene work, discounted
rows.explainer: Each year's benefit at the shared discount rate.

rows.label: Value of a diarrhoeal death averted
rows.explainer: The site's age split of diarrhoeal deaths in Sub-Saharan Africa (facts/death_ages.json, WHO GHE) by the site's values by age.

rows.label: Deaths averted per person given water (before adjustments)
rows.explainer: Deaths averted per person given water (before adjustments).

rows.label: Value of water-fetching time saved, as a share of consumption
rows.explainer: Where CARE brings water closer it saves households fetching time, mostly women's and girls'; much of its water work is hygiene and repairs that save little time. 0.5% of consumption per person (0-2%), half World Vision's borehole figure.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person from time saved, over the water point's life
rows.explainer: ln(consumption) gain per person from time saved, over the water point's life.

rows.label: Consumption gain for a savings-group member's household
rows.explainer: Randomised trials of savings groups, several of them CARE's own: Ksoll et al. 2016 (CARE's VSLAs in Malawi) found more meals a day and more consumption; Karlan et al. 2017 (PNAS, CARE, Oxfam and Plan in Ghana, Malawi and Uganda) found more savings, small business gains and women's empowerment but no detectable consumption gain on average; Beaman et al. 2014 (Mali) similar. Enterprise and market work adds a little for fewer people. 1.2% (0-4%), under World Vision's 1.5% whose livelihoods line includes some graduation work.

rows.label: Years the gain lasts
rows.explainer: Groups keep meeting after support ends (most survive in follow-ups); gains are modest and fade. 2 years (1-4).

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person, discounted
rows.explainer: ln(consumption) gain per person, discounted.

rows.label: Consumption gain per household member reached by food security and resilience work
rows.explainer: Farmer field schools and input support raise yields and income a few percent in reviews (Waddington et al. 2014, Campbell); nutrition counselling and climate-resilience work add less in consumption. 2% (0-6%).

rows.label: Years the food security gain lasts
rows.explainer: New farming practices partly persist after projects end. 2 years (1-4).

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per person, discounted
rows.explainer: ln(consumption) gain per person, discounted.

rows.label: Learning gain per child or young person reached (standard deviations)
rows.explainer: Community-based schools in Afghanistan raised test scores and enrolment a lot in trials (Burde and Linden 2013), but much of CARE's education reach is short girls' leadership and life-skills courses with little measured learning. 0.06 SD (0.01-0.15).

rows.label: Adult earnings gain per SD of learning
rows.explainer: Returns to test scores in low-income countries run 10-20% a SD in wage studies; fewer of these children reach waged work. Judgment 15% (5-30%).

rows.label: Share of the learning gain that lasts into adulthood
rows.explainer: Test-score gains fade by half or more within a few years in most follow-ups. Judgment 40% (20-80%).

rows.label: Years from the programme to adult work
rows.explainer: Children are mostly 6-12 years old. Judgment 10 years (6-14).

rows.label: Working years the gain lasts
rows.explainer: GiveWell's shared figure for later-life income gains.

rows.label: Household members sharing the earnings gain
rows.explainer: GiveWell's shared figure.

rows.label: ln(consumption) gain per child reached, discounted to today
rows.formula: ln(1 + education_learning_gain_sd * education_earnings_per_sd * education_persistence) * pv_annuity_due(1, $discount_rate, working_years) * (1 + $discount_rate) ^ (0 - education_years_until_work) * resource_sharing_multiplier
rows.explainer: ln(1 + learning gain × earnings per SD × persistence) for each working year, discounted, after the wait to adult work, shared with the household.

rows.label: US foreign aid kept or added per dollar of public information, credited to CARE
rows.explainer: CARE's public information and its lobbying arm CARE Action press for the US aid budget alongside hundreds of groups; the budget fell sharply in 2025 regardless (USAID closed, a rescission). Most of this line is public education, not lobbying. Judgment $0.30 of aid per dollar (0-3).

rows.label: Value of a dollar of US aid, as a multiple of cash to the poor
rows.explainer: The site's shared value of a dollar of a rich country's aid budget whose use isn't known more exactly (facts/aid_value.json): about 1× @cash.uov_per_dollar (0.4-2×), a mix of global health aid at GiveWell's Global Fund and Gavi figures, humanitarian aid at a fifth of cash and other development aid at about half. The same figure in every model that values aid won or kept.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, relief deaths averted
rows.explainer: Applies to the deaths averted only: they rest on weak evidence, already wide in share_excess_averted, and the studies are of other settings. The goods' value needs no effect study and isn't discounted here. 0.85 (0.7-1).

rows.label: Counterfactual, relief
rows.explainer: Whether the people reached would have been helped anyway: UN humanitarian appeals were well under half funded in 2025 after the US cuts, and food pipelines in Sudan, Ethiopia and Yemen ran at part rations, so another agency would rarely have filled the gap; but some of CARE's WFP and US food would have gone through another partner to the same people. 70% (45-90%).

rows.label: CARE's share of the resources behind the deaths averted
rows.explainer: The deaths averted come from the whole response the people got: part is US government and WFP food that CARE distributes, whose procurement, shipping beyond the $12.8M of freight on CARE's books, storage and staff are outside CARE's costs, and local partners and other agencies add their own services. 80% (65-95%).

rows.label: CARE's share of the resources behind the goods' value
rows.explainer: The goods are valued at a share of CARE's own spending (relief_goods_value_share), so the donors' off-book costs don't enter the value counted; only local partners' and volunteers' own contributions to delivering it do. 95% (85-100%).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, health
rows.explainer: The newborn effect comes from trials of intensive packages under study conditions; CARE's version runs at scale through community health workers and government clinics with no published mortality evaluation. 0.5 (0.3-0.8), as for World Vision.

rows.label: Counterfactual, health
rows.explainer: Government health services and other agencies cover part of the same mothers. 80% (60-95%).

rows.label: CARE's share of the resources behind the health outcomes
rows.explainer: CARE trains and supports government community health workers and clinics, whose salaries and medicines are mostly the government's. 55% (35-80%).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, water
rows.explainer: The effect is from meta-analyses of interventions like CARE's; uptake at scale is lower than in trials (already partly in the effect). 0.7 (0.5-1).

rows.label: Counterfactual, water
rows.explainer: Governments and other agencies would have reached some of the same communities. 80% (60-95%).

rows.label: CARE's share of the resources behind the water outcomes
rows.explainer: Communities contribute labour, materials and repair funds. 80% (60-95%).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, savings groups
rows.explainer: The gain is from trials of CARE's own model, but small and uncertain, already in the range of the gain. 0.8 (0.5-1).

rows.label: Counterfactual, savings groups
rows.explainer: Groups spread by themselves in some villages (replication), so some members would have joined one anyway. 85% (65-100%).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, food security
rows.explainer: The gain is from reviews of farmer training with wide variation; CARE's programmes have uncontrolled evaluations. 0.7 (0.4-1).

rows.label: CARE's share of the resources behind the food security gains
rows.explainer: Farmers' own inputs and labour are theirs (not a co-funder's), but government extension workers and co-funded projects share in the training. 85% (65-100%).

rows.label: Counterfactual, food security
rows.explainer: Government extension and other agencies reach some of the same farmers. 85% (65-100%).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, education
rows.explainer: The learning gain is from trials of somewhat different programmes and the chain to earnings is long. 0.6 (0.3-1).

rows.label: CARE's share of the resources behind the education gains
rows.explainer: Community-based schools use community-provided space and are later taken over by government teachers; girls' programmes run with schools. 80% (60-100%).

rows.label: Counterfactual, education
rows.explainer: Some children would have been schooled anyway, though CARE works where girls are kept out of school. 85% (60-100%).

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (fidelity, compliance, follow-through)
rows.explainer: Reach is CARE's own count or a judgment from its spending; aid diverted, people counted twice and programmes delivered below design. CARE is audited by Ernst & Young and its US grants by the single audit. In 2025 US stop-work orders in 32 countries ended about $130M of active awards early (FY2025 annual report, letter from the CFO), so some of the year's spending bought half-finished work: 3 points below the usual 85%. 82% (65-95%), for every branch.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Private money is fungible across CARE's programmes, and other CARE members may give less where CARE USA gives more (below 1); private funds sometimes unlock matching public grants (above 1). 1 (0.9-1.05).

rows.label: Missing-data discount, relief
rows.explainer: Thin: CARE USA publishes no count of the people its own spending reached; reach is its spending at the confederation's cost per person, and the deaths averted rest on the research on food and cash in crises. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Missing-data discount, health
rows.explainer: Thin: reach is spending over a judged cost per birth and the effect is from trials of other packages; no mortality evaluation of CARE's programmes. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Missing-data discount, water
rows.explainer: Thin: reach is spending over a judged cost and the effect from meta-analyses of other programmes. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Missing-data discount, livelihood
rows.explainer: Thin: the effect is from randomised trials of CARE's own savings groups, but reach is spending over a judged cost per member. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Missing-data discount, food
rows.explainer: Thin: reach is spending over a judged cost and the effect from reviews of other farmer programmes. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Missing-data discount, education
rows.explainer: Thin: reach is spending over a judged cost and the effect from trials of other programmes. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Missing-data discount, awareness
rows.explainer: Thin: no outcome data; aid kept is a judgment. So it is counted less by the shared slider, the same way in every model (docs/normalization.md 2.12).

rows.label: Side effect: illness averted by emergency health, nutrition and protection services
rows.explainer: Part of the relief is emergency health care, malnutrition treatment and gender-based violence services, whose illness averted isn't in the deaths or the goods' value; relief is about three-fifths of the result. +3% (0 to +8%).

rows.label: Side effect: women's say and safety from savings groups and gender work
rows.explainer: Savings-group trials find gains in women's say in household decisions and in coping with shocks (Karlan et al. 2017), not valued in consumption; CARE puts women at the centre of its work. +2% (0 to +5%).

rows.label: Side effect: food aid's harm to local farmers' prices
rows.explainer: Imported US food aid can lower local grain prices near distributions; most is in deficit areas where the effect is small, and CARE gives more cash than in-kind food. -0.8% (-2.5% to 0).

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: The signed side effects above, each sized against the branch it belongs to; funging is in leverage_funging_adj and health work's own illness in its morbidity share, so neither is counted here again.
